Abbot:
The maker Jack. G. Abbot started making banjos around 1890 under his own name but made for various other makers and outlets including Barnes and Mullins, Norton Greenop and Sanders and Papworth. Examples of these banjos are held in the collection and can be fund under the relevant collection name.

At around the time of the late 19th Century and for years onwards many mainstream makers of the time made banjos and did not mark them which allowed other outlets to brand them.

Abbot was a fine maker and made quality banjos. An interesting feature of Abbot banjos was the style of the peg head. The shape remained the same throughout his lifetime and is an aid to identifying an Abbot made banjo.
Barnes and Mullins:
Samuel Bowley Barnes and Edward Mullins are known to be making banjos from circa1894. They were both also players, they advertised in early journals such as ‘The Joe’ which later became the more famous ‘Troubadour’. Their banjos were made for them by J. G Abbot, W. Temlett, Windsor and Matthews reducing the number of banjos they themselves produced and made.

In 1960 -65 their banjos were made in Germany and marketed as Barnes and Mullins.
Bostock: T. Bostock of Ransom St, Clerkenwell, London was wholesale maker of banjos and zither banjos from around 1880. Bostock a marvellous maker and craftsman, his banjos have the most wonderful sound. Beautiful banjos and a personal favourite of the makers held within this collection.
Brewster:
JE Brewster emigrated from Newfoundland in 1872 to the UK and shared a workshop with JE Dallas for a few years. Brewster was a rogue and well have made banjos but these examples of banjos are where the manufacturer’s name has been rubbed out and Brewsters stamp applied as if his own. The case with SS Stuart is well documented. A JB Schall banjo within this collection is stamped as Brewster.

Writer of music and performer including of music halls. Though Brewster was not well liked by other makers, his reputation preceded him but he was a brilliant musician until 1900 and perhaps beyond. During one performance, local makers such as Dallas got into trouble for disrupting one of his concerts. Brewster left the UK and lived in Paris. His legacy is banjos with a Brewster name arouse suspicion as a result of his dubious activities.
Bacon: TW Bacon of London around 1882, Bacon imported his parts from Dobson USA and assembled his banjos with great skill.
Barratt: Late 19th Century original maker of Dobson banjos. Stamped ‘George Barratt original maker of Dobsons Brooklyn UC New York’.
Wilmshurst: London late 19th Century around 1890 better known for his exquisite zither banjos.
Bertolli: JC Bertolli – In the 1880’s was playing and teaching banjo. His banjos made by Dexter Company – very little known about these but a certainty that Richards Spencer a master of English banjos made for Dexter. In 1898 Bertolli formed a playing partnership with Gordon Tate calling themselves the Dexter’s and made their debut at a Cameyer Concert.
Boileau: Charles Chamberlain Boileau a little known American maker out of New York around 1880.
Buckbee: J. H Buckbee of New York America rumoured to have had the largest factory and output at its peak making ten thousand banjos each year! From around 1860 to mid to late 1890’s and made banjos for Dobson and JW Wallis. Buckbee label not found so perhaps the firm didn’t market instruments under their own name other than a JHB on the side of the heel.
Butler: George Butler and early English maker 1798 – 1867
Cammeyer:
Alfred D Cammeyer came from America in approximately 1885. Started a workshop and regarded as the maker of the first zither banjos and indeed made well crafted and beautiful zither banjos. This craftsmanship also extended and evident in his open backed banjos.

At one time he did form a partnership with Clifford Essex but dissolved the partnership in 1900. Cammeyer did make thousands of banjos in total always held in high esteem.

Later on Sidney Young worked with Cammeyer on producing his banjos. Making banjos from 1890 onwards. Always tell a Sidney Young made instrument because of the craftsmanship as one of the finest banjo makers.
Clamp: John Clamp of Newcastle cabinet maker by trade but appears to start making banjos around 1890. He didn’t produce a great volume compared to other makers but probably made around 30 per year. There is not a lot known about John Clamp.
Clerc:
Leon Clerc, born in London 1864, age of 18 playing ‘Star Minstrels’ at 22 he became an established teacher in the East End of London. In 1888 he opened a factory 44 – 48 Shoreditch Street, London. His main model number the ‘Athena’ 88EHA, the ‘Crescent’ and the ‘Marvel’.

Clerc continued to play and formed the Athena Quartet which promoted his banjos. Production of Clerc banjos ceased circa 1908. All his banjos were exceptional with 3 in the collection.
Deane: A.W. Deane of Reading Berkshire, believed he had banjos made for him as he did by makers such as Windsor but it has come to light that Deane also made exquisite banjos. There is a fine example on the vintage banjo makes website.
Essex: First started with Alfred D Cammayer forming a partnership in 1893 for teaching studios dissolving in 1900 and although Clifford Essex models were made by other makers at the time they did make fantastic banjos in around 1904 with Alfred Dare as foreman and notably Will Mitchell. Essex made banjos are exquisite. On the demise of Alfred Weaver eses and Cammayer brought his stock and turned out Weaver banjos which were difficult to distinguish between actual Weaver made banjos.
GHS: GHS 5 string made around 1938 GHS involved J Dallas’s sons and G Houghton and produced some really top quality 5 string banjos.
Hewitt: Hewitt patent banjo around 1900 made by Stainer Banjo Company which consisted of Hewitt his wife and daughter and were made on premises at the rear of their home by them. Fantastic design and quality. Note the tuning peg design.
Miller: A late 19th Century Miller, suspect he worked for W. Temlett one of our early makers. This example around 1867 it was wrecked but restored, originally a 7 string but was held for only a short time as restored for Dave Johnson at the Mosely Violin Centre and another rare and high quality banjo.
Morris:
This is a rare and remarkable banjo very rare made by George Morris around 1885. It is one of the most pleasurable banjos to play with fantastic tone and volume.

Scale 27inches pot 12 inches. George Morris was renowned for the quality of his banjos and anyone who has one never sells. Waited 30 years to get one!
Nice: One of our earliest commercial makers from his workshop in Eccleston St, London. Nice later moved to premises in Fleet St. It’s interesting that Will Mitchell went to R. Spencer later and then on to Cliford Essex where he ran the workshop.
Norton Greenop: A late 19th Century made by Abbott Greenop a player and writer. Played a duo with A Stanley senior; played every music hall in the UK a couple of times and played in South Africa until they stopped in 1914.
Spratt:
This is a Harry Spratt around 1870 the panel on the fretboard is old style engraved as is the tension ring. It’s marked Spratt very rare banjos.

Pot is 11 inch and 5/8 inch the construction is really lovely and tend to go for incredible money.
Taylor: Walter Taylor from Liverpool was a gunsmith and started designing and making banjos in around 1879 one of the most innovative makers. Every banjo has a different design but his banjos are always very decorative, outstanding quality, quite rare and much sought after. Each banjo is a one off, very individual with special features.
Winder: J.G Winder who was advertised as a pioneer maker of mandolins and guitars in Great Britain. This late 19th Century example is from around 1890 estimated and is a superb construction. The pot is 11inches and 3/8’s. 26.6 inch scale. Typical Winder peghead and a blind rim on the tension ring which takes the hooks beneath the velum. A rare example.
